newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's Pick sees strong meat exports.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's Pick sees strong meat exports.

text.p: Hungarian meat food processor Pick Szeged Rt general director Vilmos Bihari said on Wednesday the company expects to continue export growth while maintaining domestic dominance.
"From the data we have in our possession we are now able to bring about our major plans for the year," Bihari told Reuters following a news conference to discuss the company's third quarter results.

Pick, Hungary's leading maker of salami and other processed meat products, announced on November 11 an operating profit of 1.937 billion forints for the first nine months of 1996, up from 1.48 billion forints for the same period of 1995.

Bihari said the company had accomplished this despite high prices for hogs at the beginning of the year, a change in export subsidies and the continued decline in purchasing power in the Hungarian market.
He said exports had powered Pick's growth, rising to 7.707 billion forints from 5.502 billion forints in the same period last year.
"We more than doubled the meat exported and we maintained our position in the stable markets like Germany, Austria and Sweden," Bihari said.
"We have also been able to produce some growth in the so-called CEFTA countries like Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia and Slovenia."
In addition, Bihari said Pick had succeeded in re-opening its business in Russia, which once was a huge market for the company that ended when communism collapsed and Russia had problems paying.
Bihari said Pick was expanding its product lines to include a new range of prepared, frozen foods, but he said the company would not lose sight of the flagship winter salami for which it is famous.
"The strategy is to maintain the leading article as the winter salami and the selling of this product as a quality brand with availability at the right time and the right price," he said.
Bihari said he was pleased that several investment houses, among them CS First Boston and Nomura, had recently rated Pick as a "buy."
Pick's issues lagged well behind the Budapest Stock Exchange's key BUX index this year, growing 12 percent against a 100 percent rise in the index.
Bihari said this was mostly due to investor concern about the meat sector because of the fears of mad cow disease, and doubts about companies dealing with the depressed Hungarian consumer sector.
"But in my opinion, everything is ship-shape at Pick," he said. "And I strongly believe that our stock will now outpace the index."
